phonemes.desc: [u], a smooth rounded close back vowel; the initial digraph simply marks the sound [u].
Tapped or trilled [r] followed by open [a].
Acute stress on the antepenult; the i is short and sharp.
Final long [aː], giving the name its feminine nominative ending.

pronunciation.approximation: 'oo-rah-NEE-ah' — stress the third syllable and let the final 'ah' lengthen slightly.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Οὐρανία, 'the heavenly one', feminine of Οὐρανός, Sky.

kin.label: Latin
kin.form: Urania, adopted directly into Roman poetry and astronomy.

kin.label: Modern use
kin.form: Astronomical societies, observatories, and planetariums still bear her name.

pronunciation.note: Ouranía is Tier 1: the Greek original has both acute stress and a long final vowel. The Roman spelling Urania drops the distinctive breathing and accent, making the PUNICODEX form the fuller restoration.

domains.title: Muse of Astronomy
domains.subtitle: Heavenly Song and the Starry Discipline
domains.lead: Ouranía is the Muse of astronomy and the heavenly sphere. While her sisters preside over history, comedy, and dance, she lifts the poet's eye to the stars. In Hellenistic and Roman art she appears with a celestial globe and compass, the patron of mathematics married to music.

cards.name: Celestial Globe
cards.desc: She holds a sphere of the heavens, mapping constellations and the dance of planets.

cards.name: Compass of Ratios
cards.desc: Astronomy was geometry; her compass divides the circle into measured arcs.

cards.name: Harmony of Spheres
cards.desc: The Pythagorean belief that the stars move to mathematical music she guards.

cards.name: Muse of Kings
cards.desc: She inspires rulers to look upward and order earthly affairs by celestial law.

symbols.name: Celestial globe
symbols.meaning: The universe reduced to a sphere, symbol of astronomical knowledge.

symbols.name: Compass
symbols.meaning: The instrument of measurement that turns the sky into geometry.

symbols.name: Star crown
symbols.meaning: Her dominion over the fixed stars and wandering planets.

symbols.name: Scroll or tablet
symbols.meaning: The written tables of risings and settings that govern the calendar.

mythology.lead: Ouranía's mythology is quiet but persistent. She is less a protagonist than a presence: the mind that turns the chaos of stars into cosmos.

myths.title: Birth of the Muses
myths.text: Hesiod names Ouranía as one of the nine Muses born from Zeus and Mnēmosýnē, Memory. They were conceived in nine nights of union and born in nine days, each goddess receiving a province of the arts and sciences. Ouranía received the sky and the mathematical wonder it provokes.

myths.title: The Heavenly Muse
myths.text: In the Homeric Hymn to the Muses and in Roman poetry, Ouranía is invoked at the start of astronomical or philosophical poems. She is the one who can make number sing, who can translate the cold march of planets into verse worthy of the gods.

myths.title: Ouranía and Aphrodítē
myths.text: Some sources distinguish Aphrodítē Ouranía ('Heavenly Aphrodite') from Aphrodítē Pándēmos. The name Ouranía thus carries a philosophical charge: heavenly love, ordered and contemplative, set against the common love of the marketplace. The Muse and the goddess share a word for the same reason: both draw mortals toward what is above them.

lore.syncretism: Roman poets and astronomers adopted Ouranía/Urania without significant alteration, and the Renaissance restored her as an allegory of the new mathematical sciences. Christian writers saw in her globe and compass an emblem of divine order. In the modern era her name labels observatories, learned societies, and even a planetarium software, so that the ancient Muse has become the face of scientific astronomy itself.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ouranía is the muse who survived the scientific revolution. Every observatory named Urania, every astronomical society that invokes her, testifies to the persistence of the idea that studying the stars is not mere calculation but a form of contemplation. She stands at the intersection of poetry and physics, reminding us that the heavens were humanity's first text.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Ouranía teaches an ancient discipline: look up. In an age of downward-glancing screens, her domain is a call to recalibrate. The stars do not need us, yet we have always needed them—for navigation, for calendar, for the sense that our small lives are part of a larger pattern.

To invoke Ouranía is to refuse the split between art and science. The same wonder that named constellations also calculated orbits. The same reverence that composed hymns to the Muses also built the first telescopes. She is the patron of anyone who has ever looked at the night sky and felt, for a moment, that the universe makes sense.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Greek name is Οὐρανία, the feminine form of Οὐρανός ('Sky'). The initial Oὐ- marks a smooth breathing before the vowel [u]; the acute accent on -ní- indicates the stress falls on the antepenult. The final -α is long in the nominative singular. PUNICODEX writes Ouranía with the acute accent and the breathing implied, since domain registries reject the smooth breathing mark itself but accept the accented Latin transcription.
